answer.rationale: The binding constraint is not cost alone but cost under zero delivery slack: the line is at 94% of committed volume, the contract lapses in 14 days, and I get exactly one move. That rules out the actions that create transition exposure. memory_c2 (switch to low-cost vendor) is the only lever that plausibly delivers an 18% cut on its own, so it is the memory worth spending my single verification on — and precisely because it is the most tempting, it deserves the most scrutiny. It is dated 'last year,' says nothing about whether that vendor was carrying primary volume at this scale, and 'onboarding was quick' plus 'invoicing stayed accurate' are administrative signals, not evidence of allocation resilience under a tight ramp. If the source record shows the cost win came at lower volume or with buffer inventory absorbing the changeover, switching in a 14-day window with no buffer is a delivery-risk bet dressed up as a savings decision. So I intend negotiate_terms: memory_c4 records that benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and memory_c6 records that longer commitments unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service scope — combined, those are a credible path to a real cost reduction with no migration work (memory_c1) and no gap at expiry. I am explicit that this likely does not reach the full 18% by itself; add_second_source (memory_c3) is the natural next-cycle move once the primary is secured, and I would rather under-deliver on the mandate than convert a spend target into a stockout. Two value risks I want on the record rather than buried: chasing the 18% purely on unit price can quietly trade away service scope, quality tolerances, or supplier relationships that do not appear in a TCO line item; and a multi-year commitment taken to hit this year's number reduces future optionality, including the ability to dual-source later. All six memories are consolidated summaries with sources archived — they report what worked in one prior context, not what generalizes here, and the two most confident-sounding ones point in opposite directions, which is itself a reason to hold uncertainty rather than resolve it by picking the boldest claim.
